New machine. Its objects are: kativo, gifeses, nirebon, ponogen, pofazi, genefa.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: kativo, gifeses, nirebon
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group didn't light the machine, but I don't know the rule yet. Testing the other three objects should help tell whether one nexiom is enough to light it, or whether it needs both.

TEST: ponogen, pofazi, genefa
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit up. If one nexiom were enough, one of the halves would have lit. So the rule probably needs both nexioms, and they must be split across the halves: one in {kativo, gifeses, nirebon} and one in {ponogen, pofazi, genefa]. That leaves 9 possible pairs. Two tests give only 4 possible outcomes, so I can't be sure of narrowing it to one pair. This test splits the candidates as evenly as I can: it lights if the pair is in {kativo, gifeses} × {ponogen, pofazi}, which is 4 of the 9.

TEST: kativo, gifeses, ponogen, pofazi
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

After three dark results, I'm working on the assumption that the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it. That is the simplest rule that fits, but other rules could also fit.

The first two tests then mean one nexiom is in {kativo, gifeses, nirebon} and the other is in {ponogen, pofazi, genefa}. The third test rules out every pair inside {kativo, gifeses} × {ponogen, pofazi}. That leaves 5 possible pairs:
- nirebon + ponogen
- nirebon + pofazi
- nirebon + genefa
- kativo + genefa
- gifeses + genefa

One test has only two outcomes, so I can't narrow 5 pairs down to one for certain. My chance of being right ends up about 2 in 5 whichever test I pick. So I'll test a single pair directly. If it lights, I know the answer. If not, I'll guess among the remaining four.

TEST: nirebon, genefa
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

All four tests came back dark, so I can't identify the pair with certainty. Assuming the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it, the last test rules out nirebon + genefa. That leaves four equally likely pairs:
- nirebon + ponogen
- nirebon + pofazi
- kativo + genefa
- gifeses + genefa

This is a guess with about a 1 in 4 chance of being right. That's lower than the 2 in 5 I estimated before the last test, because that figure counted the chance the test would light. It also depends on the "needs both" rule, which fits the results but was never confirmed, since the machine never lit up.

ANSWER: nexioms = nirebon, ponogen
One last question. If only nirebon were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**No**, nirebon alone almost certainly would not light the machine.

- **Under the "needs both" rule I assumed:** one object can never light the machine on its own, whether or not it's a nexiom.
- **Under a "lights with any nexiom" rule:** test 1 included nirebon and stayed dark, so nirebon couldn't be a nexiom. It wouldn't light alone either.
- **Under an "exactly one nexiom" rule:** all four dark results would only fit if the pair were kativo + gifeses or ponogen + pofazi. Nirebon wouldn't be a nexiom, so again no light.

Every rule I can think of that fits the four dark results predicts no light for nirebon alone. That doesn't rule out some stranger rule I haven't considered.

PROBE: no

Testing duvenen and furavu together settles it:

- **If it stays dark:** the nexioms are lopoti + furavu.

The plan has one weakness. If the rule were "one is enough," furavu would be a nexiom paired with masuful, tupivun or posipak, and this test would light anyway. I can't check both rules with one test left. My notes and the results so far favour "needs both," so I'm going with it.

TEST: duvenen, furavu
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

The last dark result rules out duvenen + furavu, which leaves **lopoti + furavu**. That pair fits all four results:
- **Test 1 (duvenen, lopoti, furavu, masuful) lit:** both nexioms were on the machine.
- **Test 2 (duvenen, lopoti, furavu) lit:** both nexioms were on the machine.
- **Test 3 (duvenen, lopoti) dark:** only lopoti was on, without furavu.

This last result also settles the rule. Under "one is enough," tests 3 and 4 being dark would mean duvenen, lopoti and furavu are all non-nexioms. Test 2 would then have stayed dark, but it lit, so "one is enough" is ruled out. A rule of "lights only with exactly one nexiom" fails the same way. "Needs both" is the only rule I considered that fits all four results, and it gives exactly one pair.

ANSWER: nexioms = lopoti, furavu
One last question. If only furavu were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**No.** Test 4 already answers this. Duvenen and furavu together stayed dark, and if lopoti and furavu are the nexioms, duvenen has no effect on the machine. So furavu alone should behave exactly like test 4 and stay dark.

This also fits the "needs both" rule: one nexiom by itself isn't enough to light the machine.
